Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
You can never know who will harm you

vignette:
Valentina Reyes is a 59-year-old divorced Latina woman who works as a project manager for a mid-sized construction firm. She was referred for psychological assessment following a PCL-5 score of 77, placing her in the severe range for post-traumatic stress symptoms. She presented as guarded but articulate, describing an event that occurred fourteen months ago and from which, she said quietly, she had not yet returned.

Valentina had been working late at a downtown office building when she was taken by two men who forced her into a locked utility room on the building's lower floor. She was held there for nearly eleven hours - the door bolted from the outside, no windows, no phone signal - before a security guard discovered her the following morning. During those hours she was physically restrained, and at several points struck across the back of her neck and shoulders when she attempted to call out. She was not sexually assaulted, but she was made to believe repeatedly that she would not leave the room alive. By the time she was found, she had spent the better part of a night certain she was going to die in a space no larger than a closet.

In the months that followed, Valentina found that the world had reorganised itself around that room. At work, she began avoiding the conference rooms with heavy doors and no interior handles - a reasonable enough precaution at first, she told herself, but one that gradually expanded. Now she reroutes her path through the office to avoid any corridor where a door might close behind her. When a colleague inadvertently locked a shared workspace during a meeting, Valentina left without explanation and did not return to that floor for a week. The sensation of having no options - no exit, no recourse - is the most reliable way to collapse the distance between the present and that utility room, and her body responds before her mind can intervene. Her neck pain, a residual injury from those hours of restraint, flares unpredictably; when it does, she is no longer in a project meeting or sitting at her desk but back on the cold floor, and the alarm that follows is immediate and total. These triggers reliably activate a state of heightened threat, her heart rate climbing, her attention narrowing to exits and obstacles in a way that her colleagues have begun to notice.

What has made this harder to bear is what Valentina has come to believe about what the experience means. She had come to believe she was no longer the person she used to be - that the woman who had once managed complex projects with confidence and warmth was simply gone. She described herself as feeling dead inside, as if the capacity for ordinary pleasure had been sealed off. More than that, she was now certain that you could never truly know who intended to harm you, that safety was a story people told themselves. This conviction - that threat was ambient and unknowable - kept her permanently braced, unable to relax even at home, scanning rooms and faces for warning signs that never fully resolved. That persistent sense of danger, in turn, made her more sensitive to the very cues that had marked the original event: enclosed spaces, physical constraint, the ache in her neck. The loop was self-sustaining and exhausting.

In an effort to manage the relentless vigilance, Valentina had developed habits that offered only temporary relief. She found herself going over the details of the event compulsively, searching for the decision that would explain it, the moment she could have acted differently. She dwelt on what she had done wrong - arriving late, taking the stairs, not screaming sooner - as though the right answer would undo the helplessness she still carried. And sometimes, when the weight of it became too much, she told herself it had not really been that bad, that she was exaggerating. But these strategies left her more destabilised, not less. The rumination and the minimisation together deepened her sense that she was broken and miserable, and the unresolved threat kept her body in a state of readiness that no amount of reasoning could interrupt.

What finally brought Valentina to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago when she was unable to enter the elevator alone and stood in the lobby for twenty minutes before taking the stairs to the eighth floor, arriving late to a client presentation she had spent weeks preparing. She said she was not afraid of dying anymore. What frightened her most now was that this was simply who she had become.
